fields.expected: Something my resume doesn't show: I spent the last year independently studying how scientific research gets funded and evaluated, mostly because of something I noticed at Hopkins. A lot of very capable people around me were moving quickly toward consulting, banking, and finance, even when they didn't seem particularly interested in the work itself. That made me wonder why scientific exploration isn't one of the more attractive paths for people like that. I started by reading about the history of research institutions, from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH and NSF grant model, and then talked with researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative research organizations. My initial thesis was that compensation and grant-writing time were the main constraints. Conversations complicated both. Many researchers consciously trade money for autonomy, and I now think the bigger effect of grant review is selection: people learn which ideas are legible enough to get funded and stop attempting the ones that aren't. I wrote a Substack essay synthesizing that, and it's shaped how I think about evaluation in AI systems too.

fields.expected: I work mostly in Python and TypeScript across the model and application layers. On the modeling side I've used PyTorch (trained a CNN for facial-landmark prediction to ~95% PCK), XGBoost with SHAP for feature selection on a ~10M-record national survey dataset, and RNN/Transformer-style temporal sequence models for anomaly scoring plus a learning-to-rank layer on event streams. On the LLM side I've built retrieval-augmented generation systems using OpenAI models and embeddings, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph for memory retrieval, along with rubric-driven LLM-as-judge pipelines where separate judges score dimensions in parallel and synthesize an evidence-cited assessment. I've also designed an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. For serving and automation I've used FastAPI and Flask microservices, AWS, Supabase, SQLite, Zod for schema validation, and Playwright for browser agents built with explicit state machines and fail-closed safety gates. The part I care most about is evaluation and reliability: generating an output is cheap, deciding whether it should be trusted is the harder problem.
